concept.name: Stress testing
concept.definition: A risk management technique that evaluates the impact of severe but plausible adverse scenarios — historical replays or hypothetical shocks to prices, rates, spreads, and liquidity — on a portfolio or institution, reaching beyond what statistically calibrated models capture. BCBS principles make it both a core bank risk-management tool and a supervisory instrument.
concept.intuition: Models tell you about ordinary Tuesdays; stress tests ask what happens on the once-a-decade Wednesday that bankrupts the unprepared.
concept.mechanics: Define objectives and governance, select scenarios (historical events such as 2008, or hypothetical factor shocks), apply them to positions through re-pricing or sensitivity models, and assess losses, liquidity, and capital adequacy; results feed limits, capital planning, and contingency funding plans. The principles require sufficiently severe stresses, granular data, fit-for-purpose models, and independent validation.
concept.formula: Scenario P/L = sum over positions of (re-priced value under shocked factors - current value); no single universal formula — severity and factor design define the test.
concept.failure_modes: Stress tests are only as imaginative as their scenario designers: risks outside the chosen scenarios go unmeasured, and scenarios calibrated to the last crisis miss the next one. They also assume positions can be re-priced — in illiquid stress the very marks are hypothetical.
concept.misconceptions: Passing a stress test is not proof of resilience — it is one scenario's verdict, not a guarantee — and stress testing complements rather than replaces probabilistic measures like VaR, because tail probabilities are unreliable exactly where the test operates.
concept.example: Re-pricing a rates book under a 2008-style shock (rates -100bp, spreads +300bp, correlations toward one) to check the desk survives without breaching its capital or liquidity floor.
